back: A study technique where you review material at increasing intervals over time, exploiting the spacing effect to move information into long-term memory.
The robust finding that information studied in spaced-out sessions is retained much better than information studied in a single massed session (cramming).

front: Why does cramming feel effective even though it isn't?
back: Cramming produces strong short-term recall, creating a fluency illusion. But without spacing, the memories decay rapidly. Students mistake short-term familiarity for durable learning.

front: What is retrieval practice (the testing effect)?
back: The finding that actively pulling information from memory — via self-testing, flashcards, or free recall — strengthens memory more than passive review like re-reading.

front: Why is retrieval practice more effective than re-reading?
back: Retrieval forces the brain to reconstruct the memory, strengthening neural pathways. Re-reading only produces shallow recognition, not the deep processing needed for durable recall.

front: What is free recall and how can you use it to study?
back: After reading a chapter, close the book and write down everything you can remember. Then check what you missed. This is one of the simplest and most powerful retrieval practice techniques.
Mixing different topics, problem types, or skills within a single study session, rather than doing blocked practice (finishing all of one type before starting another).

front: Why does interleaving work even though it feels harder?
back: Interleaving forces the brain to discriminate between problem types and select the right strategy, building stronger and more flexible knowledge. Blocked practice feels fluent but doesn't build discrimination skills.

front: What is elaboration as a study strategy?
back: Generating explanations, asking 'how' and 'why' questions, connecting new material to things you already know, and creating your own examples to build richer mental models.
1) Pick a concept. 2) Explain it in simple language as if teaching a beginner. 3) Identify gaps where your explanation breaks down. 4) Go back to the source and fill the gaps. Repeat.
Pausing while reading to explain to yourself why each step or statement is true. Students who self-explain learn more deeply than those who just read straight through.
Challenges introduced during learning (spacing, interleaving, retrieval) that slow initial performance but enhance long-term retention and transfer. Coined by Robert Bjork.

No. A difficulty is only 'desirable' if it triggers beneficial cognitive processing (like retrieval or discrimination). Unrelated obstacles (noisy room, unreadable font beyond a point) are just obstacles.
Thinking about your own thinking — monitoring what you know and don't know, judging the effectiveness of your strategies, and adjusting your approach accordingly.
The mistaken belief that because material feels familiar (from re-reading), you actually know it well. It is a metacognitive error — confusing recognition with recall ability.

front: What is calibration in the context of studying?
back: How accurately your confidence matches your actual performance. Well-calibrated students know what they know and what they don't. Poorly calibrated students are overconfident or underconfident.

front: How does sleep affect memory consolidation?
back: During sleep (especially slow-wave and REM stages), the brain replays and consolidates memories, reorganizing and strengthening neural connections. Sleep deprivation significantly impairs learning.

front: Name three passive study strategies that feel effective but are NOT.
back: 1) Re-reading notes or the textbook. 2) Highlighting or underlining. 3) Copying definitions word-for-word. All create familiarity without deep processing or retrieval.
